headline: The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, which represents the Blue Cross and Blue Shield health insurers, says hospitals' AI billing tools added an estimated $942 million to its plans' costs from 2023 to 2025, a claim hospitals dispute.
score_reason: Pool 6, lowered by 2: re-dated item, the analysis ran in our 25 and 27 Sep 2026 editions and the hospitals' reply in our 6 Oct edition; no new fact seen on 16 Oct.
importance_line: If the claim holds, insurers and employers, and in time patients through higher premiums, are paying more for diagnoses that did not change care, but it is the insurers' own analysis, hospitals say sicker patients explain it, and no one has reviewed medical records to show which codes came from AI.
summary: Quartz reported in late September 2026, as relayed by Yahoo, that an analysis by the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, carried in our 25 and 27 Sep 2026 editions, estimates AI billing software raised its member insurers' spending by about $942 million from 2023 to 2025 by finding extra secondary diagnoses, which move hospital claims into higher payment categories even when care does not change. The American Hospital Association, the main US hospital trade group, answered on 5 Oct 2026 (our 6 Oct edition) that the analysis did not review medical records or show which claims involved AI and that older, sicker patients explain the more complex coding.
notes: RE-DATED: the analysis ran in our 25 and 27 Sep 2026 editions (Quartz 28 Sep, CNBC 1 Oct) and the hospitals' reply in our 6 Oct 2026 edition; the 16 Oct Telehealth.org item adds no new fact we could see.
